prompt: Which of these is a non-functional requirement?
explanation: A latency target describes how well the system must perform, not what feature it provides, so it is a non-functional requirement. The others are features (functional requirements).

options.text: A user can shorten a long URL
The redirect must complete in under 100 milliseconds
A user can delete their account
The system emails a receipt after purchase

prompt: What is the difference between a fault and a failure?
explanation: A fault is a single component going wrong. A failure is the system as a whole failing to do its job. Fault-tolerant design keeps faults from becoming failures.

options.text: A fault is a user error; a failure is a bug
A fault is one component misbehaving; a failure is the whole system not delivering its service
A fault happens in testing; a failure happens in production

prompt: Which three properties does Designing Data-Intensive Applications use to frame good systems? Select all that apply.
explanation: DDIA frames system design around reliability, scalability, and maintainability. Profitability is a business concern, not one of these three.

prompt: The single component that limits the whole system's performance is called the ______. (one word)
explanation: The bottleneck is the limiting component; improving anything else won't help until you address it.

prompt: A team with zero users builds sharded databases and a dozen microservices 'to be scalable.' What is the main problem?
explanation: Scalability trades against simplicity, maintainability, and cost. Designing for load you don't have buys complexity you must pay for now.

options.text: Nothing — you can never be too scalable
They traded away simplicity, maintainability, and cost to solve a problem they don't have yet

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
explanation: Latency is per-request time; throughput is volume over time; reliability is correctness under faults; maintainability is the human cost of running and evolving the system.

pairs.right: How long a single request takes
How many requests are handled per unit of time
Keeping working correctly when faults occur
How easily people can operate and change the system

prompt: Which statement best captures the difference between latency and throughput?
explanation: Latency is per-request time; throughput is volume over time. Adding parallel workers can raise throughput without changing per-request latency.

options.text: Latency is requests per second; throughput is time per request
Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how many requests complete per unit of time
They are two names for the same measurement
Latency applies to reads; throughput applies to writes

prompt: Why do engineers report p99 latency instead of the average?
explanation: A few very slow requests drag the average in a misleading way. p99 shows what the slowest 1% of requests actually experience.

options.text: The average is harder to compute
p99 is always smaller, so it looks better
The average hides the slow tail that real users experience

prompt: Approximately how much downtime per year does 99.99% availability (four nines) allow?
explanation: Four nines allows roughly 52.6 minutes of downtime per year. Three nines is ~8.8 hours; five nines is ~5.3 minutes.

prompt: Match each reliability term to its meaning.
explanation: The SLI is measured, the SLO is the target you hold it to, the SLA is the contractual promise (usually looser than the SLO), and the error budget is 100% minus the SLO.

pairs.right: A measured indicator of service quality
The internal target for an indicator
A customer contract with consequences
The amount of failure the SLO permits

prompt: Which are true of scaling out (horizontal scaling)? Select all that apply.
explanation: Scaling out adds machines, avoids a single-machine ceiling, and can be fault-tolerant — but it brings distributed-systems challenges. Consistency is not free; it is one of those challenges.

options.text: It spreads load across more machines
It can be made fault-tolerant with no single machine as a hard ceiling
It always guarantees strong consistency for free

prompt: If your SLO is 99.9% success, the 0.1% of allowed failure is called your ______ ______. (two words)
explanation: The error budget is 100% minus the SLO — the amount of failure you are allowed to spend on risk and change.

prompt: Approximately how many seconds are in a day?
explanation: A day is 24 x 60 x 60 = 86,400 seconds, roughly 10^5 — a handy shortcut for turning per-day numbers into per-second (QPS).

prompt: What is the main lesson of the classic latency numbers?
explanation: The ratios matter: memory (~100 ns) << SSD (~tens of microseconds) << disk seek (~10 ms), and a cross-continent round trip (~150 ms) dominates. That is why we cache and use CDNs.

options.text: All storage is about equally fast
Memory is far faster than SSD, which is far faster than disk, and a cross-continent round trip dwarfs local work
Network calls are always faster than memory access
Disk seeks are measured in nanoseconds

prompt: A service handles 40 writes/second. Assuming a 100:1 read-to-write ratio, what is the approximate read QPS?
explanation: read QPS = write QPS x read:write ratio = 40 x 100 = ~4,000 reads/second.

prompt: Because traffic is spiky, you should always size a system for its ______ load, not its average. (one word)
explanation: Sizing for the average under-provisions; apply a peak factor (often 2-3x) and design for the peak.

prompt: Which factors belong in a storage estimate? Select all that apply.
explanation: Storage = items x size per item x retention x replication factor. Forgetting replication is a common way to undercount by a factor of 2-3.

prompt: What makes a back-of-the-envelope estimate trustworthy and defensible?
explanation: The value is order-of-magnitude, not precise. Stated assumptions are what let others verify and challenge the estimate.

options.text: Reporting the number to several decimal places
Stating the assumptions behind it so others can check them

prompt: Which best describes what IP guarantees?
explanation: IP handles addressing and routing but is best-effort. Reliability and ordering are added by TCP on top of IP.

options.text: Reliable, ordered delivery of every packet
Addressing and routing on a best-effort basis, with no delivery guarantee

prompt: When is UDP a better choice than TCP?
explanation: UDP is connectionless and low-overhead. For live media, delivering on time beats delivering everything, so a lost packet is skipped rather than resent.

options.text: When every byte must arrive in order (e.g., a file download)
When timeliness matters more than guaranteed delivery (e.g., live video)
When you need automatic retransmission of lost data
When you need a reliable connection handshake

prompt: What does TLS add on top of HTTP? Select all that apply.
explanation: TLS provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. It does not change how packets are routed.

options.text: Authentication of the server via a certificate

prompt: DNS answers are stored for a period defined by their ______, so most lookups are served from cache. (acronym or word)
explanation: The TTL (time-to-live) controls how long a DNS answer is cached before it must be looked up again.

prompt: A service makes 10 sequential calls to a database across an ocean, each a ~100 ms round trip. Why is this slow regardless of database speed?
explanation: Ten sequential round trips add up to ~1 second no matter how fast the database is. Batch the calls or co-locate the components.

options.text: Latency is dominated by the number of round trips, so 10 x ~100 ms = ~1 second of pure network time

prompt: How does a CDN reduce latency for a global audience?
explanation: A CDN serves cached content from an edge location close to the user, turning a ~150 ms trip to the origin into a few milliseconds.

options.text: It caches content on edge servers near users, so requests reach a nearby edge instead of a distant origin
It removes the need for DNS

prompt: Which of these HTTP methods are idempotent? Select all that apply.
explanation: GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — repeating them has the same effect as doing them once. POST is not idempotent.

prompt: What does it mean that GET is a 'safe' method?
explanation: A safe method is read-only. GET (and HEAD) retrieve data without changing server state.

options.text: It is read-only and does not change server state

prompt: Why does a POST that charges a customer's card need an idempotency key?
explanation: Because POST is not idempotent, a retry could create a second charge. An idempotency key lets the server return the original result instead of acting again.

options.text: POST is not idempotent, so a network retry could charge twice; the key lets the server recognize the retry

prompt: Match each API style to what it is best suited for.
explanation: REST suits public resource CRUD, gRPC suits efficient internal RPC, and GraphQL lets clients request precisely the data they want.

pairs.right: Public CRUD APIs over resources
Fast internal service-to-service calls
Rich clients fetching exactly the fields they need

prompt: A client requests a user that does not exist. What should the API return?
explanation: 404 Not Found precisely communicates that the resource doesn't exist. Returning 200 hides the failure and confuses clients, caches, and monitoring.

prompt: Why is cursor (keyset) pagination usually better than offset pagination for very large, changing datasets?
explanation: Deep offsets get slower the further you page and shift when items are inserted. A cursor points to where you left off, staying fast and stable.

options.text: It returns more results per page
It stays fast and stable as data grows and changes, while deep offsets get slow and shift
It does not require a database

prompt: What does the 'A' in ACID guarantee?
explanation: Atomicity means a transaction fully succeeds or fully fails — a half-completed transfer never persists.

options.text: Availability — the database is always up

prompt: Match each NoSQL family to what it is best at.
explanation: Each NoSQL family targets a data shape: key-value for lookups, document for whole records, wide-column for write-heavy large tables, and graph for relationships.

pairs.right: Ultra-fast lookups by a single key
Flexible, self-contained records read as a whole
Very high write volume over large tables
Relationship-heavy queries and traversals

prompt: Is the claim 'SQL databases can't scale, only NoSQL can' accurate?
explanation: Relational databases scale with replicas and partitioning (and distributed SQL); NoSQL scales by giving up features like joins and multi-key transactions. The difference is trade-offs, not a hard limit.

options.text: Yes, relational databases cannot scale at all
No — it's an oversimplification; they make different trade-offs

prompt: You need multi-row transactions and complex joins for an orders-and-payments feature. Which fits best?
explanation: Money and multi-row integrity call for ACID transactions and joins, which relational databases provide natively.

prompt: Using more than one type of database in a single system, each chosen for a workload, is called ______ persistence. (one word)
explanation: Polyglot persistence means picking the right store per workload rather than forcing everything into one database.

prompt: In ACID, whose responsibility is the 'C' (consistency) largely considered to be?
explanation: As DDIA notes, the C in ACID is largely the application's responsibility: it defines the invariants, and the database enforces the constraints it's told about.

options.text: The application's — the database enforces the constraints you declare

prompt: In the cache-aside pattern, what happens on a cache miss?
explanation: On a miss, cache-aside reads the source (database), populates the cache, and returns the value, so subsequent reads hit the cache.

options.text: The application reads from the database, stores the result in the cache, and returns it
The cache blocks all other reads

prompt: What is the main risk of write-back (write-behind) caching?
explanation: Write-back acknowledges the write after updating the cache and flushes to the database later, so a cache failure before the flush loses data. The upside is fast writes.

options.text: Data can be lost if the cache fails before flushing to the database
The cache can never be read

prompt: What does an LRU eviction policy evict when the cache is full?
explanation: LRU (Least Recently Used) drops the entry that has gone unused the longest, keeping recently accessed data available.

options.text: The entry unused for the longest time

prompt: A viral item's cache entry expires and thousands of requests miss at once, flooding the database. What is this called?
explanation: Synchronized misses on a hot key create a cache stampede. Mitigate with TTL jitter, request coalescing, and serving slightly stale data during refresh.

prompt: Which are valid ways to handle cache staleness? Select all that apply.
explanation: TTLs, explicit invalidation, and write-through are the standard tools for bounding or eliminating staleness. Not writing to the database is not a real option.

options.text: Set a TTL so entries expire
Explicitly invalidate the entry when the data changes
Use write-through to keep the cache fresh on every write
Never write to the database again

prompt: The fraction of reads served from the cache rather than the backing store is called the cache ______ ratio. (one word)
explanation: The cache hit ratio measures how often reads are served from cache; a higher ratio means more latency and load saved.

prompt: Which benefits does a load balancer provide? Select all that apply.
explanation: A load balancer gives scalability, availability, and better latency. Durability of data is a storage concern, not something a load balancer provides.

options.text: Sending requests to less-busy or closer servers (latency)

prompt: What distinguishes a Layer 7 load balancer from a Layer 4 one?
explanation: Layer 4 routes on IP and port without reading content; Layer 7 reads the application protocol (HTTP), enabling content-based routing and TLS termination, at the cost of more processing.

options.text: Layer 7 is always slower and never used
Layer 7 understands the application protocol and can route on HTTP path, host, headers, or cookies

prompt: Requests vary widely in duration (fast lookups and slow reports). Which algorithm balances them best?
explanation: Least-connections sends each new request to the least-busy server, smoothing uneven load that round-robin would distribute blindly.

prompt: What does a health check let a load balancer do?
explanation: Periodic health checks detect failing servers so the load balancer stops sending them traffic, turning a crash into a non-event for users.

options.text: Automatically remove unhealthy servers from rotation and route around failures

prompt: Why is relying on sticky sessions often a design smell?
explanation: Stickiness papers over server-side state. Making servers stateless (shared session storage) lets any server serve any user and survive failures.

options.text: They pin users to one server, so a failure loses their state and load can't rebalance freely

prompt: A component whose failure takes down the whole system is called a single ______ of failure. (one word)
explanation: A single point of failure (SPOF) is why production runs redundant load balancers — the component that provides availability must not be able to take the system down.

prompt: What makes a service 'stateless'?
explanation: Stateless means no per-client memory is kept on the server between requests; state lives in a shared store or in the request, so servers are interchangeable.

options.text: It never stores any data anywhere
It keeps no per-client state between requests, so any instance can serve any request

prompt: Where can you move state to make a service stateless? Select all that apply.
explanation: State can go to a shared database, a distributed cache, object storage, or travel with the client as a token. Local memory is exactly what makes a service stateful.

options.text: A signed token carried by the client

prompt: Match each AKF Scale Cube axis to what it means.
explanation: X duplicates the whole app, Y splits by function (services), and Z splits by data (sharding). Real systems combine all three.

pairs.right: Clone the whole app behind a load balancer
Split the system into separate services by function
Partition the data so each node handles a subset

prompt: Which scaling axis does statelessness most directly enable?
explanation: Cloning the whole app (X-axis) only works if instances are interchangeable, which requires statelessness.

prompt: A service writes uploaded files to local disk. Why does this break when scaled out?
explanation: Local disk is state tied to one server. Using shared object storage keeps the service stateless so any server can serve any request.

options.text: Local files are per-server state, so a follow-up request on another server won't find them
Files cannot be uploaded over HTTP
It doesn't break; local disk is shared automatically

prompt: Splitting a system into separate services by function corresponds to the ______-axis of the AKF Scale Cube. (single letter)
explanation: The Y-axis is functional decomposition — splitting by function into independent services, the road toward microservices.

prompt: In leader–follower replication, where do writes go?
explanation: All writes go to the leader (primary), which applies them and replicates the changes to its followers. Reads may use followers.

options.text: Only to the leader, which streams changes to followers

prompt: What is the main risk of fully asynchronous replication when the leader fails?
explanation: Asynchronous replication acknowledges a write before followers have it, so a leader crash can lose those un-replicated writes on failover.

options.text: Recent writes not yet replicated can be lost during failover
The followers become leaders automatically with no data

prompt: A user updates their profile, then immediately reloads and sees the OLD value. What is happening?
explanation: The read hit a follower that hadn't caught up to the leader (replication lag). Routing the recent writer's reads to the leader for a short window fixes it.

options.text: A read-your-writes anomaly caused by reading a lagging follower

prompt: What is 'split brain' in a replicated database?
explanation: Split brain happens when a failover promotes a new leader but the old one is still active (just unreachable), so two leaders accept conflicting writes and corrupt data.

options.text: A database split across two regions
Two nodes both acting as leader and accepting conflicting writes

prompt: Which are valid reasons to replicate a database? Select all that apply.
explanation: Replication provides availability, read scaling, and geographic proximity (and durability). It complements but does not replace backups.

options.text: High availability if a node fails
Keeping a copy near users to reduce latency
Eliminating the need for backups entirely

prompt: The delay before a follower catches up to the leader's latest writes is called replication ______. (one word)
explanation: Replication lag is how far behind a follower is; it causes read anomalies like read-your-writes and non-monotonic reads.

prompt: What is the main goal of partitioning (sharding)?
explanation: Partitioning splits data across nodes so total storage and write capacity grow with the number of nodes. It is usually combined with replication, not a replacement for it.

options.text: To keep a full copy of all data on every node
To split the dataset so each node holds a subset, letting capacity grow with the cluster
To remove the need for replication

prompt: What problem does consistent hashing specifically solve?
explanation: Consistent hashing minimizes data movement when the node set changes — only ~K/N keys relocate. Even load still requires virtual nodes.

options.text: It minimizes how many keys must move when a node joins or leaves (~K/N)
It guarantees perfectly even load with no extra mechanism
It encrypts keys before storing them

prompt: What are virtual nodes (vnodes) for in consistent hashing?
explanation: A few physical nodes on a ring can split it unevenly. Placing each node at many ring positions (vnodes) smooths the distribution.

options.text: To balance load by placing each physical node at many points on the ring

prompt: Why does partitioning by a timestamp key often create a hotspot?
explanation: With a monotonic key like a timestamp, every new write lands on the newest partition while older partitions sit idle — a classic hotspot.

options.text: All new writes share the newest timestamp, so they all hit the single newest partition
Timestamps are too large to store

prompt: One celebrity's shard receives 1000x the reads of any other. Does better hashing fix it?
explanation: Hashing balances many keys, not one red-hot key. Mitigate a hot key by caching it or splitting it across sub-keys.

options.text: Yes, hashing always balances load perfectly
No — this is a single hot key, not skewed distribution; you need caching or key splitting
Yes, if you add more virtual nodes
No, the data must be deleted

prompt: Why is 'hash(key) mod N' a poor way to assign keys to nodes?
explanation: With mod N, adding or removing a node changes N and remaps nearly all keys, causing huge data movement and cache churn. Consistent hashing avoids this.

options.text: It is too slow to compute
Changing N remaps almost every key at once, causing a massive reshuffle

prompt: What does linearizability (strong consistency) guarantee?
explanation: Linearizability is a recency guarantee on single objects: the system appears to have a single up-to-date copy, and reads never see stale data once a write completes.

options.text: Replicas converge only if writes eventually stop
The system behaves like one up-to-date copy: once a write completes, later reads see that write or a newer one
Transactions run one at a time in some serial order

prompt: Which statement about linearizability vs serializability is correct?
explanation: Linearizability concerns real-time recency of single-object operations; serializability concerns transactions appearing to run in some serial order. Both together is strict serializability.

options.text: They are two words for the same thing
Linearizability is single-object recency (real-time order); serializability is transaction isolation (some serial order). They are independent.

prompt: Which consistency model is the strongest that still stays highly available during a network partition?
explanation: Causal consistency preserves cause-and-effect ordering and can remain available under partition, unlike linearizability which requires coordination.

options.text: No consistency is available during a partition

prompt: Is the 'C' in ACID the same as the 'C' in CAP?
explanation: They are different ideas: ACID's C is about the integrity constraints the application defines; CAP's C is linearizability, a replication recency guarantee.

options.text: Yes, both mean the same consistency
No — ACID's C is application integrity constraints; CAP's C is linearizability

prompt: Match each consistency guarantee to its promise.
explanation: Each guarantee targets a specific anomaly: seeing your own writes, not moving backward, eventual convergence, or full real-time recency.

pairs.right: You always see your own most recent writes
Successive reads never go backward in time
Replicas converge if writes stop
Reads always see the latest write, as if one copy

prompt: A 'is this username taken?' check must never let two people claim the same name. Which model does it need?
explanation: Uniqueness requires seeing the very latest state so only one claimant wins — that is linearizability. Eventual consistency could let both succeed.

prompt: What does the CAP theorem actually say?
explanation: CAP is specifically about behavior during a partition: you must sacrifice either consistency or availability while partitioned. The rest of the time you can have both.

options.text: A distributed system can only ever have two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
During a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability
Consistency and availability are impossible together, always

prompt: Why is 'pick 2 of 3' a misleading way to state CAP?
explanation: Networks fail, so a distributed system must tolerate partitions. You don't trade away P; you choose C or A when a partition occurs.

options.text: Because partition tolerance isn't optional for a distributed system, so the real choice is C vs A during a partition
Because there are actually four properties

prompt: During a partition, how does an AP system behave?
explanation: An AP system favors availability: it answers from whatever nodes are reachable, accepting possibly stale data, and reconciles once the partition heals.

options.text: It refuses requests to stay consistent
It answers requests from reachable nodes, possibly returning stale data
It guarantees the latest data on every read

prompt: A teammate says 'our distributed database is CA — consistent and available, no partition tolerance.' What's wrong?
explanation: Partitions are unavoidable in a distributed system, so 'giving up P' isn't real. The system must decide CP or AP for partition behavior.

options.text: Nothing, CA is the best choice
You can't opt out of partitions in a distributed system, so CA isn't a meaningful choice — you must pick CP or AP
CA means the system is always down
CA only applies to single-node caches

prompt: What does PACELC add beyond CAP?
explanation: PACELC: if Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency — capturing that strong consistency costs latency even without partitions.

options.text: It removes the need to choose during a partition
It adds the normal-operation trade-off: Else (no partition), choose Latency or Consistency
It says availability is always best

prompt: In the CAP theorem, what does 'C' (consistency) specifically mean?
explanation: CAP's C is linearizability, a recency guarantee — distinct from ACID's C, which is about application integrity constraints.

options.text: The ACID integrity constraints of a transaction
Linearizability — every read sees the most recent write

prompt: What is a key difference between a message queue and an event log (like Kafka)?
explanation: A queue removes each message on consume (workers compete); a log retains ordered messages so many consumers read independently by offset and can replay history.

options.text: A queue keeps messages forever; a log deletes them immediately
A queue removes a message once consumed; a log retains ordered messages that consumers read by offset and can replay
A log can only have one consumer

prompt: What is the main downside of at-least-once delivery?
explanation: At-least-once never loses messages, but a lost acknowledgment can cause redelivery, so consumers may see duplicates and must handle them idempotently.

options.text: The same message may be delivered more than once (duplicates)
It cannot be used with queues

prompt: Why is true exactly-once DELIVERY generally impossible in a distributed system?
explanation: The ambiguity of a missing acknowledgment forces a choice between at-most-once (risk loss) and at-least-once (risk duplicates). Exactly-once delivery can't be guaranteed.

options.text: Because a sender with no acknowledgment can't tell if the message or the ack was lost, so it must risk loss or duplication

prompt: How do real systems achieve 'exactly-once processing'?
explanation: At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer (or dedup by message id) means processing a duplicate has no extra effect — 'effectively once.'

options.text: By combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent (or deduplicating) consumers

prompt: Does Kafka's 'exactly-once semantics' guarantee exactly-once end-to-end to an external database or email service?
explanation: Kafka's exactly-once (idempotent producer + transactions) applies within Kafka. End-to-end exactly-once to an external sink still requires that sink to be idempotent.

options.text: No — it holds within Kafka; writing to an external system still needs an idempotent sink
No, Kafka has no exactly-once features at all

prompt: Coping when producers push faster than consumers can handle is called ______. (one word)
explanation: Backpressure covers buffering, scaling consumers, or slowing/rejecting producers. Unbounded queues hide overload, so monitor consumer lag and cap growth.

prompt: After a request times out with no response, what do you actually know about the outcome?
explanation: A timeout is ambiguous: the client can't tell whether the operation ran and the response was lost, or the request never arrived. This is why blind retries are dangerous.

options.text: It's unknown — the operation may have succeeded and the reply was lost, or it never arrived

prompt: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
explanation: Jitter randomizes the wait so a crowd of clients spreads their retries over time instead of hitting the recovering service in a synchronized wave.

options.text: So clients that failed together don't retry in lockstep and re-overload the service

prompt: How does an idempotency key make a non-idempotent write (like a charge) safe to retry?
explanation: The same key is sent on every retry; the server recognizes it and returns the stored result, so the charge happens at most once.

options.text: The server records the key's result and returns it on a retry, instead of performing the operation again

prompt: What is a 'retry storm'?
explanation: Synchronized, unbounded retries pile load onto a service exactly when it's weakest, often finishing it off. Backoff, jitter, retry caps, and circuit breakers prevent it.

options.text: Many clients retrying a failing dependency at once, amplifying load and cascading the failure

prompt: What is the risk of setting a timeout too long?
explanation: An overly long timeout leaks resources on a dead dependency, which can cascade into a wider outage. Too short, and you get false failures. Tune deliberately.

options.text: Threads, connections, and memory stay tied up waiting on a dead peer, risking resource exhaustion

prompt: Which operations are naturally safe to retry without special handling? Select all that apply.
explanation: GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent, so repeating them has the same effect as doing them once. POST is not idempotent and needs an idempotency key.

options.text: PUT (replace a resource with a full new value)

prompt: Why is the token bucket algorithm so widely used for rate limiting?
explanation: A token bucket refills at a steady rate up to a capacity, so a client can burst up to the bucket size but is held to a steady long-run rate.

options.text: It allows short bursts up to the bucket capacity while enforcing a steady average rate

prompt: What is the boundary-burst problem with fixed-window rate limiting?
explanation: Because the counter resets at the window boundary, a client can pack a full window on each side of the boundary, sending roughly double the intended rate in a short span.

options.text: A client can send a full window just before the reset and another full window just after, briefly doubling the rate

prompt: What HTTP status code should a rate-limited request receive?
explanation: 429 Too Many Requests signals rate limiting, ideally with a Retry-After header so well-behaved clients back off.

prompt: Which are typical responsibilities of an API gateway? Select all that apply.
explanation: A gateway handles cross-cutting concerns: routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS, and observability. It should not become the system of record for business data.

options.text: Authentication and rate limiting at the edge
Storing the primary copy of all business data

prompt: You run 5 gateway instances, each enforcing '600/minute per user' with a local counter. What goes wrong?
explanation: Local counters don't coordinate, so a user spread across N instances gets N times the limit. A shared counter (e.g., in Redis) enforces one global limit.

options.text: A user can hit each instance separately, getting up to 5x the intended limit

prompt: How does a leaky bucket differ from a token bucket?
explanation: A leaky bucket drains at a constant rate, smoothing bursts (with queuing delay), while a token bucket permits bursts up to its capacity.

options.text: A leaky bucket allows unlimited bursts
A leaky bucket queues requests and processes them at a fixed rate, smoothing bursts into a steady stream
A leaky bucket never limits anything

prompt: What is the core trade-off of adopting microservices?
explanation: Microservices buy independence (scaling, deploys, tech, teams) at the price of network calls, partial failure, eventual consistency, and operational overhead.

options.text: They are always faster to build than a monolith
They enable independent scaling, deployment, and team autonomy, but impose full distributed-systems complexity
They remove the need for databases

prompt: How should you draw microservice boundaries?
explanation: Boundaries should follow business capabilities (bounded contexts), and each service should own its data so services can evolve independently.

options.text: By technical layer (a database service, a logic service)
Around business capabilities / bounded contexts, with each service owning its own data

prompt: What is a 'distributed monolith'?
explanation: A distributed monolith has the operational cost of microservices and the coupling of a monolith: coupled deploys, shared databases, and long synchronous chains.

options.text: Services so tightly coupled that they must be deployed together or share a database — the worst of both worlds
A monolith deployed to many servers
A microservice with its own database

prompt: Why do many experts recommend starting with a monolith?
explanation: Early on the correct service boundaries aren't clear; splitting too soon cements the wrong ones. A modular monolith scales a long way and can be extracted incrementally.

options.text: You don't yet know the right boundaries, premature splitting locks in wrong ones, and a good monolith scales far

prompt: What does Conway's Law imply for microservice design?
explanation: Conway's Law says system structure reflects org structure. Aligning service boundaries with team boundaries reduces coordination friction.

options.text: Services should be as small as possible
A system's structure mirrors the organization's communication structure, so align services with teams
All services must use the same language

prompt: Which are signs of the distributed-monolith anti-pattern? Select all that apply.
explanation: Coupled deploys, shared databases, and long synchronous chains are the smells. Independent data ownership and deployment is the opposite — the healthy pattern.

options.text: You can't deploy one service without deploying others
Multiple services share the same database tables
One request fans out through a long synchronous chain of services
Each service owns its own data and deploys independently

prompt: What is a cascading failure?
explanation: A cascade is when one slow or failed dependency exhausts a caller's resources, dragging down everything that depends on it — the failure most resilience patterns aim to contain.

options.text: One failure tying up a caller's resources and taking it down, which takes its callers down, spreading across the system
A single server crash with no wider effect

prompt: In the OPEN state, what does a circuit breaker do?
explanation: When open, the breaker fails fast so callers don't pile up on a down dependency, giving it room to recover. After a cooldown it goes half-open to test recovery.

options.text: Fails fast — rejects calls immediately without hitting the dependency — for a cooldown period

prompt: What does the bulkhead pattern isolate?
explanation: Bulkheads give each dependency its own resource pool, so a single hung dependency exhausts only its pool and the others keep working — like watertight ship compartments.

options.text: Resources like thread/connection pools, so one hung dependency can't exhaust all of them

prompt: A product page's recommendation service is down. Graceful degradation means:
explanation: Graceful degradation returns a reduced but working response — here, the product page minus the optional recommendations section — rather than failing the whole request.

options.text: Return a 500 error for the whole page
Render the product page without recommendations instead of failing entirely

prompt: What problem does service discovery solve?
explanation: Instances constantly change (autoscaling, deploys, failures), so addresses aren't fixed. Service discovery (a registry, DNS, or platform mechanism) returns healthy instances at runtime.

options.text: Finding a healthy instance of a dependency at runtime as instances come and go

prompt: Under severe overload, why might a system deliberately reject some requests (load shedding)?
explanation: Trying to serve everything under overload can cause total collapse. Load shedding sacrifices some (often low-priority) requests to keep the core healthy for the rest.

options.text: Because serving all requests badly can collapse the system; shedding excess protects the core so most requests succeed

prompt: Why is two-phase commit (2PC) generally avoided across microservices?
explanation: 2PC provides atomicity but blocks: participants hold locks between voting and the decision, a coordinator failure strands them in-doubt, and it isn't partition-tolerant — bad for availability at scale.

options.text: It loses data on every commit
It is blocking — participants hold locks awaiting the decision, and a coordinator crash leaves them in-doubt — and it isn't partition-tolerant

prompt: What is a saga?
explanation: A saga breaks a distributed operation into local transactions; if a later step fails, compensating transactions semantically undo the completed steps.

options.text: A single ACID transaction across many databases
A sequence of local transactions where failures trigger compensating transactions to undo earlier steps

prompt: What guarantee do sagas give up compared to a single ACID transaction?
explanation: Each saga step commits immediately, so other operations can observe intermediate states. Sagas provide a form of atomicity via compensation but not isolation.

options.text: Isolation — intermediate states are visible before the saga completes

prompt: Match each saga coordination style to its description.
explanation: Orchestration centralizes the flow in one coordinator; choreography is event-driven and decentralized.

pairs.right: A central coordinator tells each service what to do next
Each service emits events that trigger the next, with no central controller

prompt: What is the dual-write problem?
explanation: Because the database and the message broker are separate systems, a naive 'write DB then publish' can leave them inconsistent if one succeeds and the other fails.

options.text: Updating a database and publishing an event are two systems that can't be written atomically, so one may succeed and the other fail

prompt: How does the transactional outbox solve the dual-write problem?
explanation: The business change and an outbox row commit together atomically; a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes (at-least-once), so consumers must be idempotent.

options.text: It publishes to the broker first, then writes the database
It writes the event to an outbox table in the SAME database transaction as the change, then a relay publishes it — so the event is sent iff the transaction committed
It uses two-phase commit between the database and broker

prompt: What is consensus in a distributed system?
explanation: Consensus is agreement on one value (or sequence) among nodes even when some fail — the basis for leader election, atomic commit, and replicated state machines.

options.text: Getting multiple nodes to agree on a single value or ordered sequence despite failures

prompt: A consensus cluster of 2f+1 nodes can tolerate how many node failures?
explanation: With 2f+1 nodes, a majority (f+1) survives f failures. For example, 5 nodes tolerate 2 failures and still form a quorum of 3.

options.text: f failures, while still having a majority

prompt: Why do consensus clusters typically run an ODD number of nodes?
explanation: 5 nodes tolerate 2 failures, but 4 nodes tolerate only 1 — the same as 3 — so the extra even node adds cost without extra fault tolerance.

options.text: A majority of an odd set tolerates the most failures per node; e.g. 4 nodes tolerate only 1 failure, the same as 3, for more cost
Even numbers can't form a majority at all

prompt: How does Raft elect a leader?
explanation: On an election timeout, a follower becomes a candidate for a new term and requests votes; winning a majority makes it leader, and it then sends heartbeats.

options.text: The node with the lowest IP always wins
A follower that hears no heartbeat becomes a candidate, increments the term, requests votes, and wins with a majority
The oldest node is always leader

prompt: What does the FLP impossibility result tell us?
explanation: FLP shows consensus can't be guaranteed under full asynchrony with a possible crash. Real systems use timeouts (partial synchrony) and sometimes randomization to make progress.

options.text: Consensus is impossible in all systems, always
In a fully asynchronous system where one node may crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee it always reaches consensus

prompt: Should you implement your own distributed leader election with a database flag?
explanation: A homegrown flag lacks the majority-overlap guarantee, so a partition can create two leaders (split brain). Use a proven coordination service that provides quorum-based election.

options.text: No — it can produce split brain under a partition; use a consensus-backed coordination service like etcd or ZooKeeper
Yes, as long as the database is fast
No, leader election is never needed

prompt: How do you remove a single point of failure?
explanation: A SPOF is removed by redundancy: running spare capacity (N+1, active-active or active-passive) so the failure of one instance doesn't take down the system.

options.text: Add redundancy — run more than one so losing one is survivable

prompt: Why must redundant copies be placed in different failure domains?
explanation: Three replicas in one rack all fail if that rack loses power. Spreading across zones/regions makes failures independent, which is the point of redundancy.

options.text: Because redundancy only helps if the copies don't fail together; copies in one rack/zone can all die at once
It doesn't matter where they are

prompt: Why is replication NOT a substitute for backups?
explanation: If a bug or bad DELETE corrupts data, replication copies the damage everywhere. A backup is a point-in-time copy that lets you recover — so you need both.

options.text: Replication faithfully propagates corruption and accidental deletes to all replicas instantly; backups are point-in-time copies you can restore from

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
explanation: RTO is downtime tolerance, RPO is data-loss tolerance; active-active runs all units live, active-passive keeps a standby ready.

pairs.right: Maximum acceptable time to restore service
Maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time
All redundant units serve traffic
A standby takes over on failure

prompt: A team runs three database replicas in the same rack 'for low latency.' What's the flaw?
explanation: Co-locating replicas in one failure domain means one rack outage takes them all down, defeating the purpose of redundancy. Spread them across zones.

options.text: They share a failure domain, so a rack power loss kills all three at once
Replicas can't be in the same rack technically

prompt: What is chaos engineering?
explanation: Chaos engineering intentionally introduces failures (killing instances, adding latency, simulating outages) under controlled conditions to prove the system's resilience before a real outage does.

options.text: Deliberately injecting failures in a controlled way to verify redundancy and failover actually work

prompt: Match each observability pillar to what it is best at.
explanation: Logs give detail, metrics give cheap aggregate trends for alerting, and traces show where a request spent time across services.

pairs.right: Detailed record of what happened at a point
Cheap aggregated numbers for trends and alerts
Following one request's path across services

prompt: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
explanation: Monitoring checks for predefined, known conditions; observability lets you answer questions you didn't anticipate, explaining unexpected behavior.

options.text: Monitoring watches for known problems; observability helps you understand new, unexpected behavior — the 'why'

prompt: What does the RED method measure for a service?
explanation: RED = Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed requests), Duration (latency) — the key user-facing signals for a request-driven service.

prompt: Why attach and propagate a trace id across services?
explanation: A shared trace id lets you jump from a spiking metric to the slow trace to the explaining log lines — reconstructing one request's end-to-end story.

options.text: To correlate metrics, traces, and logs into one story for a single request

prompt: Why should you alert on symptoms (SLOs) rather than every internal cause?
explanation: Paging on every cause (like a CPU blip) buries on-call in noise. Alerting on user-facing symptoms tied to SLOs keeps pages urgent and actionable.

options.text: Cause-based alerts create alert fatigue and non-actionable pages; symptom/SLO alerts stay meaningful and user-focused

prompt: What is a risk of using high-cardinality labels (like user id) on metrics?
explanation: Every distinct label combination creates a separate time series. High-cardinality labels like user id can generate millions of series, exploding storage and cost.

options.text: Each label combination is a new time series, so storage and cost can explode

prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
explanation: Authentication establishes identity (who you are); authorization checks permissions (what you may do). You authenticate first, then authorize each action.

options.text: Authentication verifies who you are; authorization checks what you're allowed to do
Authentication checks permissions; authorization verifies identity

prompt: How should user passwords be stored?
explanation: A per-user salt defeats precomputed-hash attacks and a slow algorithm makes brute force expensive, so a database leak exposes hashes that are impractical to crack.

options.text: As a salted hash using a slow algorithm like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2
Encrypted with a key stored next to them
As a fast unsalted MD5 hash

prompt: What is OAuth 2.0 primarily for?
explanation: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access: a user grants an app a scoped access token instead of their password. OpenID Connect adds authentication on top.

options.text: Delegated authorization — granting an app limited, scoped access to your data without sharing your password

prompt: An API authenticates users but fetches a record by id without checking ownership. What vulnerability is this?
explanation: Authentication is not authorization. Without a per-request ownership check, users can read others' records — broken access control, the most common serious web flaw.

options.text: Broken access control — any logged-in user can access others' data by changing the id

prompt: What is the principle of least privilege?
explanation: Least privilege limits each identity to the minimum access it needs, so a compromised component can do far less damage.

options.text: Give every service admin rights for convenience
Grant each user, service, and credential the minimum permissions needed and nothing more

prompt: Is a signed JWT encrypted?
explanation: A signed JWT proves integrity (it wasn't tampered with) but its payload is base64-encoded and readable. Don't store confidential data in one.

options.text: No — a signed JWT is readable (base64) and only tamper-evident, so never put secrets in it
Yes, JWTs are always encrypted by default
Only if it contains a password

prompt: What should be the FIRST step when tackling a system design problem?
explanation: Requirements (functional and non-functional) decide everything downstream. Jumping to architecture first risks solving the wrong problem or over-engineering.

options.text: Clarify the functional and non-functional requirements

prompt: Why do estimation and requirements come before drawing the architecture?
explanation: The scale estimates and requirements tell you whether you need one box or a fleet, and where caching, replicas, or partitioning are justified.

options.text: The requirements and scale numbers determine what architecture is actually needed
They slow you down on purpose

prompt: In the URL shortener, why can redirects be served with eventual consistency?
explanation: The read-heavy redirect path tolerates slight staleness, so an availability- and latency-favoring (AP-leaning) choice is appropriate. Only code uniqueness needs a strong guarantee.

options.text: Redirects must always be perfectly fresh
A newly created link appearing a moment late is acceptable, so favoring availability and low latency is a fine trade-off

prompt: Which two questions most shape where you focus design effort?
explanation: The read:write ratio and the hot path reveal whether to lean on caching/replicas (reads) or partitioning/queues (writes), and which operation must be fast.

options.text: The programming language and the cloud provider
The read:write ratio and the hot path
The team size and the deadline
The logo and the color scheme

prompt: Why generate short codes with a counter + Base62 and per-server id ranges?
explanation: Base62 of a unique id yields short, collision-free codes; handing each server a block of ids removes the hot single counter.

options.text: Base62-encoding a unique increasing id guarantees uniqueness with short codes, and per-server ranges avoid a single global-counter bottleneck
It removes the need for a database

prompt: How should you present a completed system design?
explanation: Strong designs are communicated as trade-offs (consistency vs latency, simplicity vs scale) with the bottleneck identified — there is rarely one 'right' answer.

options.text: As the single correct answer with no alternatives
As a set of justified trade-offs with the current bottleneck named
As a list of technologies only

prompt: In system capacity estimation, what power of two roughly approximates one million (10^6)?
explanation: 2^10 ≈ 1 thousand (1 KB), 2^20 ≈ 1 million (1 MB), 2^30 ≈ 1 billion (1 GB), and 2^40 ≈ 1 trillion (1 TB).

prompt: Approximately how much faster is reading from main memory (RAM) compared to reading randomly from an SSD?
explanation: RAM reference takes roughly ~100 nanoseconds, while SSD random read takes ~10–100 microseconds (10,000–100,000 ns), making memory about 100 to 1,000 times faster.

prompt: If your web service transmits 100 Megabytes per second (MB/s) of egress data, what is that bandwidth in network bits?
explanation: There are 8 bits in a byte. 100 Megabytes per second equals 800 Megabits per second (800 Mbps or 0.8 Gbps).

prompt: Why does a network round-trip from California to Europe take roughly 150 ms regardless of bandwidth?

options.text: Slow DNS server lookups at the destination
Physical limitation: the speed of light propagating through fiber optic cables

explanation: Light in fiber travels at roughly ~200,000 km/s. Over global distances (~15,000 km round trip), physical propagation delay plus intermediate router hops creates an inescapable ~100-150 ms baseline latency.

prompt: If you calculate that 10 TB of unique user data is written per year, and your database uses 3-way replication, how much raw storage must you provision per year?
explanation: With 3-way replication (one primary and two replicas), every byte of data is stored three times across distinct disks, requiring 30 TB of raw capacity.

prompt: There are 24 hours * 3,600 seconds = ______ seconds in a single day.
explanation: A day contains exactly 86,400 seconds (often approximated as 100,000 in interview calculations for fast mental math).
